title: [core-libs-dev] Feature Request -- Add ability to conditionally wrap exceptions thrown by Stream?
content:
Thread: Feature Request -- Add ability to conditionally wrap exceptions thrown by Stream?
List: core-libs-dev@openjdk.org | Messages: 1+

[OP] Hello @core-libs-dev <core-libs-dev@openjdk.org>, I am building a simple utility that searches a bunch of files for keywords. Let's assume that the act of opening a file for reading is very likely to produce an exception. Currently, my code looks something like this. record Result(Path file, String line) {} Stream<Result> search(final String keyword) { return Files .walk(Path.of(".")) .filter(Files::isRegularFile) .flatMap ( file -> { try { return Files .lines(file) .filter(line -> line.contains(keyword)) .map(line -> new Result(file, line)) ; } catch (final Exception exception) { throw new IllegalStateException("Failed for " + file, exception); } } ) ; } Now, the bug here is obvious from a glance -- that try-catch in flatMap() doesn't really do what I want. Since Streams are lazy, none of the actual file opening logic will occur inside the try-catch. Ok, there are a couple of workarounds here. The most obvious one is just to execute a terminal operation, like calling Stream::toList followed by List::stream. Now this works, but it is not clear that that is the right solution here. For starters, have I unknowingly opted-out of performance enhancements that stream could have otherwise given me? I know Streams are lazy, but I don't know "how lazy" they are. Once the body of the flatMap() lambda is reached, does it fetch the whole stream contents right away? Does it grab only a few at a time from each resulting stream, round-robin style? Something else? I could look at the code t

title: [leyden-dev] Announcement: renaming current `premain` branch to `premain-old` and creating new `premain`
content:
Thread: Announcement: renaming current `premain` branch to `premain-old` and creating new `premain`
List: leyden-dev@openjdk.org | Messages: 1+

[OP] Hi, During last Leyden meeting there was proposal to rename old `premain` branch and create new `premain` branch based on current mainline JDK. The only major project left in current `premain` branch is AOT code caching. But the current PR [1] is based on mainline JDK already and not `premain`. Merging mainline changes into leyden:premain become very complex. As result the branch was not updated in 2 months. Current `premain` branch contains experimental changes we collected for the past 3 years. Not all of them will be pushed into mainline. And we don't want to clean them up to match state of mainline JDK. It will be waste of our time and some changes could be useful in a future. We propose to rename current `premain` to `premain-old` to keep history and our experiments. And create new `premain` branch from `leyden:master` which is in sync with mainline JDK. I will push AOT code caching changes from PR to new `premain` and we may "cherry-pick` some changes from `premain-old`. This will simply merges from mainline (Valhalla when it lands in mainline) and our internal testing will continue run without need to change configuration. Please let me know other alternatives to these changes (like keeping current `premain` and creating `premain-new`, for example). Note, there will be separate e-mail after renaming is done with instructions to update your fork [2]. And for those who directly work with `premain` branch [3]. I listed instructions at the bottom. Please verify if they are

author: Evgenia Verbina

title: Alternative Structured Concurrency
content:
Java structured concurrency has been under development for a span of 5 years, weaving through 8 (!) distinct JEPs (JEP 428, JEP 437, JEP 453, JEP 462, JEP 480, JEP 499, JEP 505, JEP 525). To me, this feels rather excessive for what could be considered a fairly concise feature. 

My goal here is to experiment with an alternative approach that leverages Java's tried-and-tested, robust functionality available since JDK 1.5. It's possible this pathway could achieve better outcomes than what is proposed in JEP 505, which, from my perspective, introduces a suite of redundant interfaces and classes that replicate pre-existing ones.
